findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. Any third-party or downstream (e.g. keycloak-client repo, custom FIPS integrations) implementation of this interface will fail to compile / throw AbstractMethodError at runtime after upgrade. Give it a `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar) to keep binary/source compatibility.

findings.title: Ties in provider order are resolved non-deterministically instead of failing
findings.body: Previously, finding more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw IllegalStateException. Now providers are only sorted by `order()`, and DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If two of these end up on the classpath (a realistic misconfiguration, e.g. FIPS + default BC), the selection depends on ServiceLoader/sort stability and the server may silently run with the wrong crypto provider (e.g. non-FIPS BC in FIPS mode) instead of failing fast. Consider throwing when the top two providers have equal order, or at least logging at WARN.

findings.title: logger.debugf called with dynamic string as format
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message as a format string with no arguments. Any '%' character in a provider class name (or future message content) would cause an UnknownFormatConversionException inside logging. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", ...)`.

findings.title: Dead/duplicated ASN1 encoding calls
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write r and s, and discard the results; the actual DER is built again on lines 117-121. These two statements are dead code (wasted allocation and confusing); they should be removed.

findings.title: Test uses a default (P-256) EC key for ES384/ES512, so it does not verify real conversions
findings.body: `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the default curve (usually secp256r1) for all three tests. For ES384/ES512 the signature produced is a P-256 signature, while `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` is 96/132, so `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` silently zero-pads and the round-trip assertion passes without exercising correct ES384/ES512 behaviour. Generate the matching curve per algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and also assert that the re-derived DER signature verifies with `Signature.verify`, so a real encoding bug would be caught.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider
findings.body: The method is documented to return a BouncyCastle (FIPS or non-FIPS) security provider, but here it returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default KeyStore type. Callers such as `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` will then pass e.g. "SUN" as a provider name to algorithm lookups, which can fail with NoSuchProviderException for algorithms that provider doesn't implement. Returning null or throwing UnsupportedOperationException (consistent with the other unsupported methods) would be clearer than returning an unrelated provider.
